title: Constraints & Keep-or-Drop — Allocating a Bottleneck Across Jobs (CMA P2-C)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — one crew, two jobs, which gets the hours?

MBG's real constraint is rarely cash on a single job — it is crews and equipment. When a resource is scarce, the profit-maximizing rule is not "take the job with the highest contribution margin." It is "take the job with the highest contribution margin per unit of the bottleneck resource." This week applies the theory of constraints to allocate a bottleneck and uses relevant-cost logic to decide whether to keep or drop a line of work.

Theory of constraints — manage the bottleneck

The theory of constraints says a system's output is limited by its single tightest constraint, so throughput is maximized by exploiting that constraint and subordinating everything else to it. Throughput is sales minus totally variable cost (chiefly materials). The decision rule when one resource is scarce: rank work by contribution margin per unit of the constrained resource.

Worked allocation

Crew-hours are the bottleneck. Two illustrative jobs:

  • Job A: contribution margin $100,000, requires 500 crew-hours → $100,000 ÷ 500 = $200 per crew-hour.
  • Job B: contribution margin $80,000, requires 320 crew-hours → $80,000 ÷ 320 = $250 per crew-hour.

Job A has the larger contribution margin per job, but Job B earns $250 per bottleneck hour versus $200. With limited crew-hours, MBG fills the schedule with Job B first — it converts the scarce resource into more profit per hour. Ranking by contribution margin per job here would leave money on the table.

Keep-or-drop a segment

Whether to drop a job line, service, or division turns on avoidable costs, not allocated ones. Drop the segment only if the fixed costs saved by dropping exceed the contribution margin lost.

Illustrative: a small-renovation line generates contribution margin of $150,000 and has avoidable fixed costs of $100,000, plus $80,000 of allocated common overhead that would continue regardless. Segment margin = $150,000 − $100,000 = +$50,000. Dropping the line would lose the $150,000 contribution but save only $100,000 of avoidable fixed cost, a net loss of $50,000. So MBG keeps it. The $80,000 of allocated common overhead is irrelevant — it does not disappear when the line is dropped; it just reallocates to other lines, which can make a profitable segment look like a loser if you read fully allocated statements naively.

Subordinating to the constraint

Beyond product mix, the theory of constraints prescribes operational moves: keep the bottleneck running (avoid idle crew time), offload work from the bottleneck where cheaper (subcontract the constrained trade — connecting to week 2's make-or-buy), and elevate the constraint by adding capacity only when justified. A non-bottleneck improved in isolation adds cost without adding throughput.

CPA Crossover — decision analysis

CMA and BAR both test contribution margin per constrained unit and the keep-or-drop rule built on avoidable cost. The two classic traps: ranking by total contribution margin instead of per-bottleneck-unit, and treating allocated common fixed cost as if it were avoidable.

Practice and recap

  1. Identify the single binding constraint.
  2. Rank work by contribution margin per unit of that constraint.
  3. Keep or drop a segment on avoidable cost versus contribution margin lost.
  4. Treat allocated common overhead as irrelevant to keep-or-drop.

Recap: with crew-hours scarce, Job B's $250 per hour beats Job A's $200 even though Job A's total contribution margin is higher. And the renovation line's +$50,000 segment margin means dropping it would cost MBG $50,000 — the allocated $80,000 overhead is a distraction, not a reason.

flashcards.back: Rank work by contribution margin per unit of the constrained (bottleneck) resource.
Sales minus totally variable cost (mainly materials).

Why not rank by total contribution margin when constrained?
flashcards.back: The scarce resource, not the product, limits output; per-bottleneck-unit profit is what maximizes total profit.

flashcards.front: Is allocated common overhead relevant to keep-or-drop?
flashcards.back: No; it continues after dropping and just reallocates, so it is irrelevant.
Exploit the constraint (no idle time), offload it where cheaper, and elevate it only when justified.

questions.q: When crew-hours are the binding constraint, MBG should rank jobs by:
questions.explain: With a scarce resource, contribution margin per unit of the constraint maximizes total profit.

questions.q: Job A: CM $100,000 / 500 hours. Job B: CM $80,000 / 320 hours. Which is prioritized?
questions.explain: B earns $250 per crew-hour vs A's $200; the scarce hours go to B first.

questions.q: A line has CM $150,000, avoidable fixed cost $100,000, and allocated common overhead $80,000. Its segment margin is:
questions.explain: Segment margin = CM − avoidable fixed = 150,000 − 100,000 = +50,000; allocated common overhead is excluded.

choices: Yes; it shows a loss after full allocation
No; dropping it loses $50,000 of segment margin
questions.explain: Dropping loses $150,000 CM but saves only $100,000 avoidable cost — a $50,000 net loss; keep it.

questions.q: The $80,000 of allocated common overhead in a keep-or-drop analysis is:
choices: Relevant; it is saved by dropping
A sunk cost from last year
questions.explain: Allocated common overhead does not disappear when the segment is dropped, so it is irrelevant.

questions.q: Throughput in the theory of constraints is defined as:
questions.explain: Throughput = sales − totally variable cost (mainly materials).

questions.q: Improving a NON-bottleneck resource in isolation generally:
questions.explain: Only the binding constraint limits output; improving a non-bottleneck adds cost but not throughput.
